reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Primary carnitine deficiency is caused by defective cellular carnitine transport due to mutations in the OCTN2 (SLC22A5) transporter, impairing carnitine uptake and renal reabsorption
Presentations range from infantile hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and hepatic encephalopathy to a childhood dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy
Some individuals are identified only when a low carnitine level is found incidentally or through screening, and mothers may first be diagnosed after an abnormal newborn screen in their infant
Plasma free carnitine is markedly low, and renal carnitine wasting is characteristic of the primary transporter defect
Secondary carnitine deficiency is far more common and results from other organic acidaemias and fatty acid oxidation defects, renal loss, malnutrition, or certain drugs
Cardiomyopathy and muscle weakness in primary disease often respond well to carnitine replacement, making early recognition important
Management principle is supplementation with L-carnitine and, for secondary forms, treatment of the underlying disorder and avoidance of fasting
Detectable on newborn screening through a low free-carnitine level, which also flags affected mothers
reference.pathophysiology: Carnitine is essential for transporting long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation. In primary carnitine deficiency, loss-of-function of the OCTN2 plasma-membrane transporter prevents carnitine entry into cardiac and skeletal muscle and impairs its reabsorption in the renal tubule, causing systemic depletion and urinary carnitine wasting. Without adequate carnitine, long-chain fatty acids cannot be oxidised, so energy production fails during fasting and fatty acid-dependent tissues such as heart and muscle are especially vulnerable, producing cardiomyopathy, myopathy and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Secondary deficiency occurs when carnitine is consumed conjugating accumulated acyl groups or is lost through the kidney.
additionalDifferentials: Fatty acid oxidation defects (e.g. MCAD, VLCAD, LCHAD) causing secondary deficiency
Organic acidaemias with secondary carnitine depletion
Other causes of infantile or childhood cardiomyopathy
Nutritional or drug-induced (e.g. valproate) carnitine deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Plasma free and total carnitine (markedly low in primary disease)
Urine carnitine to demonstrate renal wasting
Plasma acylcarnitine profile and urine organic acids to exclude secondary causes
Molecular testing of the SLC22A5 (OCTN2) gene
redFlags: Acute hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy during fasting or illness
Decompensated cardiomyopathy with heart failure or arrhythmia
Sudden cardiac events in an at-risk individual
Newborn screen showing very low carnitine, which may indicate an affected and vulnerable mother
reference.prognosis: Primary carnitine deficiency generally has an excellent prognosis with carnitine supplementation, as cardiomyopathy and myopathy often reverse and metabolic crises are preventable; untreated disease, however, can cause sudden death or progressive cardiac failure. Prognosis of secondary deficiency depends on the underlying disorder.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish primary transporter deficiency from the much commoner secondary forms
Overlooking the diagnosis in unexplained childhood cardiomyopathy that could respond to carnitine
Missing an affected mother identified through her infant's abnormal newborn screen
Not investigating for an underlying fatty acid oxidation defect or organic acidaemia when carnitine is low
management: Replace carnitine as the definitive therapy with oral L-carnitine, using the intravenous route during acute decompensation
Avoid prolonged fasting to prevent hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic crisis
Expect and monitor reversal of cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy on carnitine replacement with echocardiography and ECG
Distinguish primary from secondary deficiency with an acylcarnitine profile and urine organic acids, and treat any underlying cause
Track plasma free carnitine to guide adequacy of replacement
Offer SLC22A5 (OCTN2) genetic testing, counselling and family screening, including maternal testing after an abnormal newborn screen, given autosomal recessive inheritance
